concepts.overview: The app motor lock is a Bosch feature, the eBike Lock used through the Flow app, that disables the motor when you walk away. It doesn't stop someone carrying the bike off, but it makes a stolen bike far less useful and adds a deterrent on top of a physical lock. For a commuter who will leave the bike at a rack at work, it is the feature that separates the shortlisted bikes on [theft protection](#c/01M3T6P0YK6QN24QPQNZM3WW0Q): the [Alder C5](#c/01M3T6P0YKAPP0H5Z8ZPDHW87N) supports it and the [Cedar Urban](#c/01M3T6P0YKSRD0NAXR64Y33DE8) does not. That gives the Alder its edge on this criterion. The [test ride checklist](#c/01M3T6P0YKX8CSJ7451KXV5YQ3) includes trying the lock in the app before you buy.

sections.heading: What does it actually do?
sections.md:
The lock is Bosch's **eBike Lock**, managed through the **Flow app**. When you walk away from the bike, it can disable the motor. The bike can still be pushed or carried, but without assist it is a heavy, awkward machine to ride away, which takes much of the value out of stealing it.

The Sources describe it only at this level. They don't say how the bike detects that you have left, or what happens if the phone is out of range.

The reader will leave the bike at a rack at work, so [theft protection](#c/01M3T6P0YK6QN24QPQNZM3WW0Q) is one of the four stated priorities. Other measures help, but the motor lock is the one that separates the shortlisted bikes.

- The [Alder C5](#c/01M3T6P0YKAPP0H5Z8ZPDHW87N) supports it.
- The [Cedar Urban](#c/01M3T6P0YKSRD0NAXR64Y33DE8) doesn't.

The assistant's scoring names the Alder best on theft protection because of the motor lock. The other bikes rely on locks alone. This is part of why the Alder came out as the best all-rounder.

sections.heading: How does it fit with the other theft measures?
sections.md:
The motor lock is one layer among several in [Theft & security](#c/01M3T6P0YKQF040RM3NSF4BW32), not a replacement for the others:

- A removable battery, which all four bikes have, so it can be taken inside.
- A Sold Secure Gold or Diamond D-lock plus a cable for the front wheel; see [D-lock plus front-wheel cable](#c/01M3T6P0YKP6NJWSC84AT206Q1).
- Insurance, at around 100 to 150 a year for a 3,000 bike.

The app lock is an extra deterrent on top of a physical lock, not a substitute for one.

sections.heading: What should I check before buying?
sections.md: The last step of the [test ride checklist](#c/01M3T6P0YKX8CSJ7451KXV5YQ3) is to try the motor-lock feature in the app before you buy. That confirms it works as expected with your phone and the shop's setup.

concepts.title: Test ride checklist

These criteria are what every bike in the Expedition is scored against.

concepts.title: Motors & torque
concepts.summary: Mid-drive versus hub motors, torque figures, and how the motor brands (Bosch, Shimano, Bafang) compare.
concepts.overview: This topic gathers everything about what drives the bike. The core split is between the [mid-drive motor](#c/01M3T6P0YK2NA0DWG2GY30EC7N), which sits at the pedals and works through the gears, and the [hub motor](#c/01M3T6P0YKH4AEGPF7Q4JPHQFP) in the wheel, which is cheaper and quieter but weaker on long climbs. [Torque](#c/01M3T6P0YK61ETMECKKRKQ2JJ2) is the number that separates them: 60 to 85 Nm for mid-drives against 40 to 50 Nm for typical hub motors. For a reader with an 800 m hill at about 8 percent who doesn't want to arrive sweaty, this led to [Go mid-drive](#c/01M3T6P0YK0E2NMTS3JKV4XHEY). The topic also covers the brands: [Bosch and Shimano systems](#c/01M3T6P0YKTBCA586AAMSYPRST) against [Bafang](#c/01M3T6P0YKX2MGJ6H8RBZVVSJ6), where the [dealer network](#c/01M3T6P0YK867AVZ1FN5C5XWPX) matters most.

concepts.title: Battery & range
concepts.summary: How big a battery the commute needs and how long it lasts before losing capacity.
concepts.overview: This topic covers two questions about the battery: how big it needs to be, and how long it lasts. On size, 400 to 500 Wh covers the 28 km daily [commute](#c/01M3T6P0YKF5C9G2VNH2GDY921) with a couple of days between charges, as set out under [battery size](#c/01M3T6P0YK0F27CYR8Z7YZYKNX). On longevity, [battery lifespan](#c/01M3T6P0YK8KNBKKQ7PTJ0G3QD) puts capacity at about 80 percent after 500 to 800 cycles, which may mean a replacement near year three or four. It also holds the brand debate: the idea that [Bosch batteries beat Bafang](#c/01M3T6P0YK394FYAD9D0KSYP9B) is only partly true, because [cells matter, not the brand](#c/01M3T6P0YK0CAY5WR503K636RR), and most makers buy from the same few suppliers.

concepts.title: Drivetrain, frame & maintenance
concepts.summary: Chain versus belt drive, internal gear hubs, frame style, and the upkeep each needs.
concepts.overview: This topic gathers everything about how the bike turns pedalling into motion and what it costs to keep it working. The central contrast is the [chain and cassette](#c/01M3T6P0YKRYVZKA4MYR6KHHH4), which offers more gears but needs regular cleaning and replacement, versus the [belt drive](#c/01M3T6P0YKK4A2E6K9SKJ1JZ2P) paired with an [internal gear hub](#c/01M3T6P0YKAC18NNM4VFG7J8VQ), which needs almost no upkeep but has fewer gears, slightly more friction and fiddlier tyre repairs. For a commuter who rides in rain and covers about 6,000 km a year, this choice decides how much time and money goes into maintenance. The topic also holds the [frame question](#c/01M3T6P0YKZDKKN2F08E14Q4XJ), step-through or diamond, which affects comfort with a bag and work clothes.

concepts.title: The bikes compared
concepts.summary: The four shortlisted e-bikes, how they score on the reader's priorities, and the final choice.
concepts.overview: This topic holds the shortlist and how it was judged. Four bikes in the budget were proposed: the [Alder C5](#c/01M3T6P0YKAPP0H5Z8ZPDHW87N), [Birch Metro 8](#c/01M3T6P0YK8W597PTYEB86T81R), [Cedar Urban](#c/01M3T6P0YKSRD0NAXR64Y33DE8) and the hub-motor [Dogwood Hub](#c/01M3T6P0YKRY9PC6C5WK4H7XT5), included for contrast. The first three were worth comparing closely, and were scored on the reader's priorities: hill climbing, low maintenance, weight, theft protection, then price. The result is [No bike wins everything](#c/01M3T6P0YKD4TPK5C4T6NE5EB7), and the reader picked the Alder, which answers [Which e-bike should I buy?](#c/01M3T6P0YKPDE8C5KV7TJWAE30).

This hub gathers the running costs over three years at your 6,000 km a year: chains, cassettes, brake pads and services on the chain bikes (about 850), a belt and internal hub service on the Birch (about 650), and a possible battery replacement of 600 to 800 near the end. concepts.title: Theft & security
concepts.summary: Protecting a bike left at an outdoor work rack: removable battery, locks, motor lock app, insurance.
concepts.overview: Theft worries the rider because the bike would be left at a rack at work. The chat offers four layers of defence. A [removable battery](#c/01M3T6P0YKTH7Q44G78ZXEG9GH) can be taken inside, and all four bikes have one. A Sold Secure Gold or Diamond [D-lock plus a front-wheel cable](#c/01M3T6P0YKP6NJWSC84AT206Q1) makes the bike harder to steal. An [app motor lock](#c/01M3T6P0YKDPT5M3F5NDJ5VC59) can disable the motor when the rider walks away, which the Alder supports and the Cedar doesn't. Finally, [insurance](#c/01M3T6P0YK4Y25PZD4TXP7B4V3) runs around 100 to 150 a year for a 3,000 bike. Together these feed the theft protection criterion that favours the Alder.

It matters because it is what pushed the chat toward a mid-drive rather than a hub motor. Wait, link check below. Seen another way, a good hub motor could manage 8 percent at moderate speed, but a mid-drive lets the rider shift down and keep cadence, which means less effort and, importantly for this reader, less sweat. The hill is therefore the real test for the [hill climbing](#c/01M3T6P0YK7Q97XAE9WCC76HNR) criterion, and the test ride should include riding it in the middle assist mode.

concepts.summary: Climb the 800 m, 8 percent hill easily enough to arrive at work without sweating; judged mainly by motor type and torque.

prov.quote: I really don't want to arrive sweaty

concepts.overview: Hill climbing is the reader's hardest requirement: get up one 800 m hill, at up to 8 percent, and still arrive at work without being sweaty. It is judged mainly by motor type and [torque](#c/01M3T6P0YK61ETMECKKRKQ2JJ2). A [mid-drive motor](#c/01M3T6P0YK2NA0DWG2GY30EC7N) lets you shift down and keep your cadence, so it is the safer choice, while a hub motor would cope at moderate speed but struggles on long steep climbs. Among the bikes compared, the Birch (85 Nm) and Cedar (80 Nm) are strongest, and the Alder (75 Nm) is plenty for this gradient. The [Dogwood Hub](#c/01M3T6P0YKRY9PC6C5WK4H7XT5), at 45 Nm, only partly meets the criterion. It ranks first among the four priorities the reader listed.

concepts.title: Low maintenance
concepts.summary: Little cleaning, oiling and part replacement for a daily all-weather commuter.

prov.quote: low maintenance

concepts.overview: For a daily commuter who rides in rain, low maintenance means not having to clean, oil or replace much. It is one of the reader's four stated priorities. The [Birch Metro 8](#c/01M3T6P0YK8W597PTYEB86T81R) meets it clearly, thanks to a [belt drive](#c/01M3T6P0YKK4A2E6K9SKJ1JZ2P) and internal gear hub: no oil, no rust, and a belt lasting 2 to 3 times as long as a chain. The [Alder C5](#c/01M3T6P0YKAPP0H5Z8ZPDHW87N) and [Cedar Urban](#c/01M3T6P0YKSRD0NAXR64Y33DE8) use chains that need cleaning and replacing, so they only partly meet it. The belt has trade-offs, though, and it saves only a modest amount in running costs, so this criterion competes with weight and price in [No bike wins everything](#c/01M3T6P0YKD4TPK5C4T6NE5EB7).

concepts.title: Torque
concepts.summary: The key number for hill climbing: 60–85 Nm for mid-drives (Bosch Performance Line CX 85, Shimano EP8 85, Bosch Performance Line 75) versus 40–50 Nm for typical hub motors.

overviewProv.quote: Torque is the number to look at

prov.quote: Torque is the number to look at

concepts.overview: Torque, measured in newton-metres (Nm), is the number to look at when judging how well an e-bike motor will climb. It describes how hard the motor can push at the cranks or wheel, which matters most on a steady gradient like the reader's 800 m, 8 percent hill. [Mid-drive motors](#c/01M3T6P0YK2NA0DWG2GY30EC7N) typically deliver 60 to 85 Nm: Bosch Performance Line CX and Shimano EP8 both reach 85 Nm, and the Bosch Performance Line 75 Nm. Typical hub motors give 40 to 50 Nm. Torque alone isn't the whole story, since a mid-drive also multiplies its effect through the gears, but it explains why the shortlist runs from 75 Nm on the Alder to 85 Nm on the Birch.

sections.heading: What numbers should I expect?
sections.md:
The Sources give these ranges:

- **Mid-drive motors:** 60 to 85 Nm. Examples are the Bosch Performance Line CX (85 Nm), Shimano EP8 (85 Nm) and Bosch Performance Line (75 Nm).
- **Typical hub motors:** 40 to 50 Nm.

On the shortlist, the [Birch Metro 8](#c/01M3T6P0YK8W597PTYEB86T81R) has 85 Nm (Shimano EP6), the [Cedar Urban](#c/01M3T6P0YKSRD0NAXR64Y33DE8) 80 Nm (Bafang M400), the [Alder C5](#c/01M3T6P0YKAPP0H5Z8ZPDHW87N) 75 Nm (Bosch Performance Line), and the [Dogwood Hub](#c/01M3T6P0YKRY9PC6C5WK4H7XT5) 45 Nm from its rear hub.

prov.quote: Torque is the number to look at

sections.heading: How much torque does this hill need?
sections.md:
The hill is 800 m long with a steepest grade of about 8 percent, and the rider weighs about 80 kg and carries a laptop bag. The assistant judged that a good hub motor could manage this at moderate speed. A [mid-drive](#c/01M3T6P0YK2NA0DWG2GY30EC7N) is the safer bet because the rider can shift down and keep cadence, which means less effort and less sweat, and the rider specifically wants to avoid arriving sweaty.

By the assistant's scoring, the Birch (85 Nm) and Cedar (80 Nm) are strongest on [hill climbing](#c/01M3T6P0YK7Q97XAE9WCC76HNR), while the Alder's 75 Nm is plenty for 8 percent.

sections.heading: Is higher always better?
sections.md: Not necessarily. Torque is only one input. A mid-drive drives the chain, so the gears multiply its effect on a climb, and that is part of why the Alder's 75 Nm is enough for this hill. Beyond a sufficient figure, the extra 5 to 10 Nm on the Birch and Cedar has to be weighed against the other priorities: maintenance, weight for the stairs, theft protection and price. That trade-off is why the Alder was chosen despite having the lowest torque of the three.

concepts.overview: This decision settles the motor type: go with a mid-drive. It follows from [the hill](#c/01M3T6P0YK17X3J2D1RX5XY1YZ), 800 m at up to 8 percent, and the reader's wish not to arrive sweaty. A good hub motor could manage that grade at moderate speed, but a [mid-drive motor](#c/01M3T6P0YK2NA0DWG2GY30EC7N) lets you shift down and keep cadence, so you put in less effort and sweat less. The [hub motor](#c/01M3T6P0YKH4AEGPF7Q4JPHQFP) remains the cheaper, quieter, lower-maintenance alternative, but it is the weaker climber. The decision narrows the field to the Alder, Birch and Cedar, which are compared on [hill climbing](#c/01M3T6P0YK7Q97XAE9WCC76HNR) and the reader's other priorities.

concepts.title: Bosch & Shimano systems
concepts.summary: Rated more refined by independent tests: smoother power, better sensors and software, and a larger dealer network for warranty repairs.

overviewProv.quote: Independent tests generally rate Bosch and Shimano systems as more refined

prov.quote: Independent tests generally rate Bosch and Shimano systems as more refined

concepts.overview: Bosch and Shimano are the two big-name motor systems on the shortlist: Bosch powers the [Alder C5](#c/01M3T6P0YKAPP0H5Z8ZPDHW87N) and Shimano the [Birch Metro 8](#c/01M3T6P0YK8W597PTYEB86T81R). Independent tests generally rate them as more refined than [Bafang](#c/01M3T6P0YKX2MGJ6H8RBZVVSJ6), with smoother power, better sensors and software. Their strongest advantage for a daily commuter is the larger dealer network for warranty repairs, which is the core of the claim that the [dealer network is the real point](#c/01M3T6P0YK867AVZ1FN5C5XWPX). concepts.overview: This is the question the whole Expedition serves: which e-bike suits a 14 km each-way commute with one real hill, an 80 kg rider carrying a laptop bag, and a budget up to 3,500? The conversation narrows it by first fixing the motor type, battery size and frame style, then comparing three shortlisted mid-drives against four priorities: hill climbing, low maintenance, weight for the stairs and theft protection, with price second. The reasoning rests on [no bike winning everything](#c/01M3T6P0YKD4TPK5C4T6NE5EB7): the Birch wins on maintenance and the Cedar on weight and price. Frame style, [step-through or diamond](#c/01M3T6P0YKZDKKN2F08E14Q4XJ), stays open until the test ride.

sections.heading: What was the starting point?
sections.md:
The rider commutes 14 km each way with one real hill, weighs about 80 kg, carries a laptop bag and has a budget up to 3,500. The assistant suggested starting with three choices that shape everything else: motor type, battery size and frame style. Then shortlist a few bikes and compare them on what matters.

The hill is about 800 m long and about 8 percent at the steepest, and the rider doesn't want to arrive sweaty. That pointed to a [mid-drive](#c/01M3T6P0YK2NA0DWG2GY30EC7N). A 400 to 500 Wh battery suits 28 km a day with a hill (see [battery size](#c/01M3T6P0YK0F27CYR8Z7YZYKNX)).

sections.heading: Which bikes were compared?
sections.md:
Four bikes were offered, three of them closely compared:

- [Alder C5](#c/01M3T6P0YKAPP0H5Z8ZPDHW87N): Bosch Performance Line 75 Nm, 500 Wh, 24 kg, around 3,200.
- [Birch Metro 8](#c/01M3T6P0YK8W597PTYEB86T81R): Shimano EP6 85 Nm, 504 Wh, belt drive with internal hub, 26 kg, around 3,400.
- [Cedar Urban](#c/01M3T6P0YKSRD0NAXR64Y33DE8): Bafang M400 80 Nm, 460 Wh, 23 kg, around 2,300.
- [Dogwood Hub](#c/01M3T6P0YKRY9PC6C5WK4H7XT5): a hub-motor bike included for contrast, 45 Nm, 21 kg, around 1,700.

The assistant recommended comparing the first three closely.

sections.heading: How did they score on the rider's priorities?
sections.md:
The rider named four priorities, [hill climbing](#c/01M3T6P0YK7Q97XAE9WCC76HNR), [low maintenance](#c/01M3T6P0YKV299T34JVENPH1HM), [weight for the stairs](#c/01M3T6P0YK28F35F7D5RFDFM5X) and [theft protection](#c/01M3T6P0YK6QN24QPQNZM3WW0Q), with [price](#c/01M3T6P0YKY4Y6R2G7G97ZHM6R) second. The scoring:

- **Hill climbing:** Birch (85 Nm) and Cedar (80 Nm) strongest; Alder (75 Nm) plenty for 8 percent.
- **Low maintenance:** Birch clearly, thanks to belt and internal hub.
- **Weight:** Cedar best, Alder close, Birch worst. Weight mattered because the flat is on the second floor with no lift.
- **Theft protection:** Alder best, with its [app motor lock](#c/01M3T6P0YKDPT5M3F5NDJ5VC59).
- **Price:** Cedar cheapest by about 1,000.

sections.heading: Why the Alder?
sections.md: [No bike wins everything](#c/01M3T6P0YKD4TPK5C4T6NE5EB7). The assistant called the Alder the best all-rounder for this list, the Birch the choice if maintenance matters more than the stairs, and the Cedar the choice if the rider would rather save 1,000. The rider chose the Alder. The belt's running-cost saving was modest, about 200 over three years, which weakened the case for the Birch.

concepts.title: Belt drive
concepts.summary: A carbon-reinforced rubber belt replacing the chain: no oil, no rust, lasts 2–3× as long (about 15,000–20,000 km). Needs an internal gear hub. Worth it for a rain-riding daily commuter.

overviewProv.quote: A belt drive replaces the chain with a carbon-reinforced rubber belt.

prov.quote: A belt drive replaces the chain with a carbon-reinforced rubber belt.

concepts.overview: A belt drive swaps the bicycle chain for a carbon-reinforced rubber belt. It needs no oil, doesn't rust, and lasts two to three times as long as a chain; the running-cost estimate assumes about 15,000 to 20,000 km. The catch is that a belt can't shift across cassette cogs, so it only works with an [internal gear hub](#c/01M3T6P0YKAC18NNM4VFG7J8VQ). That means fewer gears, slightly more friction, repairs that need a shop familiar with hubs, and a fiddlier flat rear tyre. For a daily rider in the rain who dislikes cleaning a chain it is attractive, and it is why the [Birch Metro 8](#c/01M3T6P0YK8W597PTYEB86T81R) scores best on low maintenance. But over three years it saves only about 200 against a chain, so the benefit is convenience rather than money.

sections.heading: How does a belt drive work, and why only with an internal hub?
sections.md:
A belt drive replaces the metal chain with a carbon-reinforced rubber belt. It needs no oil and does not rust, and it lasts two to three times as long as a chain.

The limit is in how gears work. A chain can move sideways across the cogs of a cassette, but a belt cannot. So a belt only works with an [internal gear hub](#c/01M3T6P0YKAC18NNM4VFG7J8VQ), where the gears sit inside the rear hub and the belt runs on a single fixed sprocket. The [chain and cassette](#c/01M3T6P0YKRYVZKA4MYR6KHHH4) setup is the alternative.

prov.quote: It only works with an internal gear hub (the gears sit inside the rear hub), because a belt can't shift across cassette cogs.

sections.heading: What are the trade-offs?
sections.md:
The benefits come with real costs, all tied to the internal hub it depends on:

- Internal hubs have fewer gears than a cassette.
- They add slightly more friction.
- Repairs need a shop that knows them.
- A flat rear tyre is fiddlier to fix.

The belt is therefore best seen as a convenience choice for a particular kind of rider rather than a pure upgrade. It is worth it for a daily commuter who rides in rain and does not want to clean a chain, which is why it scores well on [low maintenance](#c/01M3T6P0YKV299T34JVENPH1HM).

sections.heading: How much does it actually save?
sections.md:
In the chat's three-year estimate, at 6,000 km a year, the chain bikes (Alder and Cedar) come to about 850. That covers roughly 5 chains at 30 each, 2 to 3 cassettes at 50, brake pads and two services a year.

The belt bike, the [Birch Metro 8](#c/01M3T6P0YK8W597PTYEB86T81R), comes to about 650. A belt lasts about 15,000 to 20,000 km, so perhaps one belt (90) is needed, plus brake pads, one internal hub service (60) and yearly services.

The [three-year running cost](#c/01M3T6P0YKBCNMHWE9371W5ETG) is lower, but only by around 200. The assistant's own verdict was that this is "not a huge amount", which is the point behind the claim that the [belt saves little](#c/01M3T6P0YKQY8D4SS36JE5PH9Y). The real appeal is less cleaning and fewer parts to replace, not money.

sections.heading: Where does it fit in this decision?
sections.md: The belt drive is what sets the Birch apart on maintenance, and the Birch is the maintenance-first choice on the shortlist. It is also part of why that bike is the heaviest of the mid-drives, at 26 kg. The reader valued weight for the stairs highly and chose the Alder, which keeps a chain. The belt drive therefore remains a considered option that was weighed and set aside rather than adopted.

concepts.title: Internal gear hub
concepts.summary: Gears sealed inside the rear hub; required for a belt. Trade-offs: fewer gears, slightly more friction, needs a knowledgeable shop, and rear flats are fiddlier.

overviewProv.quote: It only works with an internal gear hub

prov.quote: It only works with an internal gear hub

concepts.overview: An internal gear hub puts the gearing inside a sealed rear hub instead of on exposed cogs, so there is no derailleur or cassette to clean or wear out. Its main role here is enabling [Belt drive](#c/01M3T6P0YKK4A2E6K9SKJ1JZ2P): a belt cannot shift across cassette cogs, so it only works with this kind of hub. The Birch Metro 8 pairs a Nexus 5 hub with a belt, which is why it scores best on maintenance. The trade-offs are fewer gears, slightly more friction, repairs that need a shop that knows these hubs, and a rear flat tyre that is fiddlier to fix. For this commuter it is the price of lower upkeep.

concepts.title: Chain and cassette

concepts.overview: The chain and cassette is the conventional way a bike turns pedalling into motion: a steel chain runs over a stack of rear cogs, and a derailleur shifts between them. It matters here because it is the baseline against which the [belt drive](#c/01M3T6P0YKK4A2E6K9SKJ1JZ2P) is judged. The [Alder C5](#c/01M3T6P0YKAPP0H5Z8ZPDHW87N) and [Cedar Urban](#c/01M3T6P0YKSRD0NAXR64Y33DE8) both use it, and it gives more gears than an internal hub. The price is upkeep: at about 6,000 km a year, the chat estimates a chain every 3,000 to 4,000 km and a cassette every other chain, plus cleaning and oiling. That adds up to roughly 850 over three years, against about 650 for the belt bike, so it feeds directly into the [three-year running cost](#c/01M3T6P0YKBCNMHWE9371W5ETG). A mid-drive also turns this chain, so it [drives through the gears](#c/01M3T6P0YKZ5G6RP8WJZE12QTT).

sections.heading: How is a mid-drive different from a hub motor?
sections.md:
A mid-drive motor sits at the pedals and drives the chain, so it uses the bike's own gears. A [hub motor](#c/01M3T6P0YKH4AEGPF7Q4JPHQFP) sits in the rear or front wheel instead and pushes the wheel directly, independent of the gearing.

The chat's comparison:

- **Mid-drive**: climbs hills far better and feels natural.
- **Hub motor**: cheaper, quieter and needs less maintenance, but struggles on long steep climbs.

sections.heading: Why does it climb better?
sections.md:
Two things combine: higher [torque](#c/01M3T6P0YK61ETMECKKRKQ2JJ2) and access to the gears. Mid-drives typically give 60 to 85 Nm. Examples given were the Bosch Performance Line CX and the Shimano EP8 at 85 Nm, and the Bosch Performance Line at 75 Nm. Typical hub motors give 40 to 50 Nm.

Because the motor drives through the gears, you can shift down on a steep section and keep your cadence. That means less effort and less sweat. An 8 percent grade over 800 m is manageable for a good hub motor at moderate speed, but the mid-drive is the safer bet.

sections.heading: What does it mean for this commute?
sections.md:
The reader has one hill, about 800 m long and up to 8 percent, and does not want to arrive sweaty. That is why the assistant recommended a mid-drive, and why the reader [went mid-drive](#c/01M3T6P0YK0E2NMTS3JKV4XHEY). The close shortlist (Alder, Birch and Cedar) is all mid-drive, with the hub-motor Dogwood included only for contrast.

The chain-driven design also has a practical consequence. Driving through the gears puts extra load on the drivetrain, which is one reason the chain and cassette remain a maintenance item on the chain bikes.

The price is weight: at 26 kg it is the heaviest mid-drive, which is hard to carry up two flights daily, and it sits near the top of the budget. sections.md:

- Motor: Bosch Performance Line, 75 Nm, mid-drive
- Battery: 500 Wh
- Drivetrain: 10-speed chain
- Equipment: mudguards and rack

sections.heading: How did it score against the reader's priorities?
sections.md:
After the reader named their priorities (hill climbing, low maintenance, weight for the stairs and theft protection, with price second), the assistant scored the bikes:

- **Hill climbing**: 75 Nm is plenty for 8 percent, though the Birch (85 Nm) and Cedar (80 Nm) are stronger.
- **Low maintenance**: the chain needs cleaning and replacing, so the Alder only partly meets this. The Birch is clearly better here.
- **Weight**: 24 kg, close to the Cedar (23 kg) and easier to carry than the 26 kg Birch. The battery can be removed first, about 2.5 to 3 kg.
- **Theft protection**: best of the three, because it supports the [app motor lock](#c/01M3T6P0YKDPT5M3F5NDJ5VC59), which the Cedar does not.
- **Price**: around 3,200, within the 3,500 budget but about 1,000 more than the Cedar.

The verdict was that no bike wins everything, and the Alder is the best all-rounder for this list.

sections.heading: What would change the choice?
sections.md: The assistant framed the alternatives by what the reader values most. The Birch is better if maintenance matters more than the stairs, and the [Cedar Urban](#c/01M3T6P0YKSRD0NAXR64Y33DE8) is better if the reader would rather save 1,000. The Cedar is also the fallback if the Alder disappoints on the test ride.

sections.heading: What should be checked before buying?
sections.md:
The reader chose the Alder in the chat, and the assistant then gave a test-ride list for confirming it:

1. Ride the hill, or a similar one, in the middle assist mode and see whether you arrive sweaty.
2. Check the frame size: stand over it with a few centimetres of clearance and reach the bars without locking your elbows.
3. Carry it up a flight of stairs with the battery out.
4. Ask about the first service (usually free after 500 km) and the battery warranty (usually 2 years).
5. Try the motor lock in the app before buying.

The full list is in the [test ride checklist](#c/01M3T6P0YKX8CSJ7451KXV5YQ3).

concepts.overview: The Cedar Urban is the budget option among the mid-drives: a Bafang M400 (80 Nm), a 460 Wh battery, a 9-speed chain, 23 kg and about 2,300, roughly 1,000 less than the others. It is the lightest bike on the list, which matters for carrying it up two flights of stairs, and its 80 Nm is among the strongest for the hill. It is the fallback if the [Alder C5](#c/01M3T6P0YKAPP0H5Z8ZPDHW87N) disappoints on the test ride, or if saving money matters more.
